title: ESR: The Westergren Method, What Moves It, and Reading the Extremes
summary: Learn how the Westergren ESR is set up and read, which patient and technical factors raise or lower it, why a normal ESR does not exclude inflammation, and how to interpret an ESR of 100 mm/h or more, including in a patient with cancer.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 31 Hits 6 and 11 and Exam Trap 4. Method details from Tuzcu 2026, Lorubbio 2024 and Amponsah 2026 (tilt figure is a secondary statement in Amponsah, citing an earlier source); factors from Lorubbio 2024, Markanday 2015 and Alende-Castro 2019; ESR ≥100 data from Markanday 2015 and Abbag 2007; normal ESR in PMR from Manzo 2018; CRP half-life from Sproston 2018. Hit 11 is qualified (register flag rv-esr-100-cancer): open sources describe an ESR ≥100 in adults with solid tumours as often associated with metastasis, but infection is the commonest cause of ESR ≥100, so “usually means metastases” omits context. Hit 11’s “temporal arteritis/polymyalgia typically >90 mm/h” could not be verified in an open source and is not taught. Not taught: Number Vault ESR limits by age band.

objectives: Describe the Westergren reference method: citrate dilution, tube, position and reading time.
List patient and technical factors that raise or lower the ESR.
Explain why a normal ESR does not exclude inflammation and interpret an ESR of 100 mm/h or more.

scenes.title: Three ESR results
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three Westergren ESR results on one shift — (1) a 72-year-old woman, ESR 38 mm/h, no symptoms; (2) a man with known colon cancer and new fever, ESR 112 mm/h; (3) a 70-year-old with new shoulder-girdle pain and morning stiffness, ESR 12 mm/h but CRP raised. Question token: “Which number means what it seems?”

cues.text: Three sedimentation rates on one shift. A seventy-two-year-old woman with no symptoms has thirty-eight millimetres per hour.
A man with known colon cancer and a new fever has one hundred and twelve. A seventy-year-old with new shoulder pain and stiffness has twelve, but a raised CRP.
Which of these numbers means what it seems to mean?

props.label: Which number means what it seems?

scenes.title: How the Westergren tube works
scenes.altText: Schematic Westergren tube (not to scale): venous blood diluted 4 volumes to 1 volume with 0.105 M sodium citrate (for example 2 mL blood + 0.5 mL citrate), drawn into a 200-mm tube, stood exactly vertical, away from vibration, and read at 60 minutes as the height of the clear plasma column in mm/h. Mechanism card: acute-phase proteins, chiefly fibrinogen, neutralise the negative charges that keep red cells apart, so cells stack into rouleaux, which settle faster. Phase strip: lag (rouleaux form) → sedimentation (near-constant fall) → packing (cells pile up at the bottom). ESR is a physical phenomenon, not a single analyte.

cues.text: The Westergren method is the reference method. Blood is diluted four parts to one with sodium citrate, about point one zero five molar. For example, two millilitres of blood with half a millilitre of citrate.
The diluted blood fills a two-hundred-millimetre tube, which stands exactly vertical, away from vibration. After sixty minutes you read the clear plasma column in millimetres per hour.

Why do cells fall? Red cells carry negative charges that keep them apart. Acute-phase proteins, especially fibrinogen, neutralise those charges, so cells stack into rouleaux, and stacks sink faster than single cells.
The curve has three phases: a lag while rouleaux form, a near-constant fall, then packing at the bottom. The result is a physical behaviour of the whole sample, not a measurement of one analyte.

scenes.title: What speeds it up, what slows it down
scenes.altText: Two columns. FASTER: high fibrinogen or globulins (infection, inflammation, pregnancy, malignancy, renal disease); anaemia (fewer red cells); older age and female sex (rough upper limit: men age ÷ 2, women (age + 10) ÷ 2); a tilted tube (a 3° tilt from vertical has been reported to raise ESR by about 30%) and vibration. SLOWER: polycythaemia; abnormally shaped cells that inhibit rouleaux formation (sickle cells, spherocytes); low fibrinogen; severe liver disease; a sample left more than about 6 hours at room temperature.

cues.text: Anything that raises fibrinogen or globulins speeds the fall: infection, inflammation, pregnancy, malignancy and kidney disease. Anaemia speeds it too, because there are fewer red cells crowding the column.
ESR also rises with age and is higher in women. A rough upper limit is age divided by two for men, and age plus ten, divided by two, for women.
Technique matters. A tube tilted just three degrees from vertical has been reported to raise the ESR by about thirty percent, and vibration raises it too.

Other things slow it. Polycythaemia thickens the blood and slows settling. Sickle cells and spherocytes inhibit rouleaux formation. Low fibrinogen, severe liver disease, and a sample left more than about six hours at room temperature all lower the result.

scenes.title: Reading the extremes
scenes.altText: Kinetics card: ESR rises within about 24–48 h of the onset of inflammation and falls back slowly; CRP is more sensitive to subtle changes and falls exponentially over about 18–20 h once the stimulus ends, close to its half-life. Normal-ESR card: 7–22% of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica have a normal ESR at diagnosis, usually with a raised CRP. ESR ≥100 card: in a large series, ESR ≥100 mm/h had low sensitivity (0.36 for infection, 0.25 for malignancy) but high specificity (0.96–0.97), and an identifiable cause was found in 90%; infection is the most common cause; in adults, solid tumours causing such values are often associated with metastasis. Hook answers: (1) 38 at 72 years is below the (72 + 10) ÷ 2 = 41 rough limit; (2) 112 is a real signal, but with fever look for infection first, do not assume metastasis; (3) a normal ESR does not exclude polymyalgia rheumatica; the raised CRP matters.

cues.text: Timing differs. ESR rises within one or two days of inflammation and falls back slowly. CRP is more sensitive to small changes and falls fast once the stimulus stops, over about eighteen to twenty hours, close to its half-life.
A normal ESR does not exclude inflammation. Between seven and twenty-two percent of people with polymyalgia rheumatica have a normal ESR at diagnosis, usually with a raised CRP.

An ESR of one hundred or more is insensitive but highly specific: a cause is found in about nine in ten. Infection is the commonest cause. In adults with solid tumours, such values are often linked with metastasis.

Back to the hook. Thirty-eight is within the rough limit for a woman of seventy-two. One hundred and twelve with fever needs a search for infection, not an assumption. And twelve does not rule out polymyalgia: the raised CRP counts.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal ESR rules out inflammation” (✓ PMR can present with a normal ESR; sickle cells, spherocytes, polycythaemia and low fibrinogen lower it); “ESR over 100 in a cancer patient means metastases, end of story” (✓ often associated with metastasis, but infection is the commonest cause of ESR ≥100 — look); “A slightly tilted tube does not matter” (✓ a 3° tilt has been reported to raise ESR by about 30%).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal ESR rules out inflammation. No: polymyalgia can present with a normal ESR, and sickle cells, spherocytes and polycythaemia pull it down.
Trap two: an ESR over one hundred in a cancer patient simply means metastases. No: metastasis is often the link, but infection is the commonest cause, so look.
Trap three: a slight tilt does not matter. No: three degrees has been reported to raise the result by about thirty percent.

scenes.title: Stacked coins sink
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “STACKED COINS SINK. Fibrinogen is the GLUE that stacks the coins (rouleaux); fewer coins (anaemia) fall faster; coins the wrong shape (sickle cells, spheres) will not stack; too many coins (polycythaemia) jam the column; and a TILTED tube lets the stack slide.” Tokens: glue = fibrinogen · wrong shape = no stack · tilt = slide. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: stacked coins sink. Fibrinogen is the glue that stacks the coins. Fewer coins fall faster. Coins of the wrong shape, like sickle cells and spheres, will not stack. Too many coins jam the column. And a tilted tube lets the stack slide.

Where it breaks: ESR also depends on vibration and sample age, and possibly ambient temperature; automated methods that extrapolate from shorter readings can differ from Westergren; and a stack of coins says nothing about which disease caused it.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Automated methods may differ from Westergren

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Westergren: 4 : 1 citrate · vertical 200-mm tube · read at 60 min”, “Normal ESR ≠ no inflammation · ESR ≥100 = find the cause, infection included”.

cues.text: The Westergren sedimentation rate measures how fast rouleaux fall in a vertical citrated tube in one hour, so red cell number and shape, fibrinogen and tilt all move it, a normal value does not exclude inflammation, and a value of 100 or more demands a search for its cause.

props.label: 4 : 1 citrate · vertical 200-mm tube · read at 60 min
Normal ESR ≠ no inflammation · ≥ 100 = find the cause

explanation.what: Plain language: the ESR measures how far red cells sink in a tall tube in one hour. When the blood has more of certain proteins, the cells stick together in stacks and sink faster, so a high ESR suggests inflammation, but many other things change it. Scientific terms: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), Westergren method, sodium citrate dilution (4:1), rouleaux, fibrinogen, globulins, lag, sedimentation and packing phases, C-reactive protein (CRP), polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).
explanation.why: Red cells normally repel one another through their negative surface charge. Acute-phase proteins, chiefly fibrinogen, neutralise that charge so cells form rouleaux, which settle faster. Fewer cells (anaemia) settle faster; more cells (polycythaemia) or cells that cannot stack (sickle cells, spherocytes) settle slower. ESR rises within 24–48 h and falls back slowly, whereas CRP falls quickly once the stimulus ends.
explanation.measure: Westergren: blood diluted 4:1 with 0.105 M sodium citrate, 200-mm tube, vertical, vibration-free, read the plasma column at 60 min (mm/h). Rough upper limit: men age ÷ 2, women (age + 10) ÷ 2. Raised by high fibrinogen/globulins, anaemia, age, female sex, pregnancy, tilt (3° reported to add about 30%) and vibration; lowered by polycythaemia, sickle cells, spherocytes, low fibrinogen, severe liver disease and delayed testing. ESR ≥100 mm/h: sensitivity low (0.36 infection, 0.25 malignancy), specificity 0.96–0.97, cause found in about 90%.
explanation.differs: ESR (indirect, physical, slow to rise and fall) vs CRP (a single protein, faster, more sensitive to small changes); true high ESR vs technical acceleration (tilt, vibration); falsely low ESR from red-cell shape or number vs genuinely absent inflammation.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify the effect of a tilted tube, name conditions that lower the ESR (sickle cell disease, spherocytosis, polycythaemia), recognise that a normal ESR does not exclude PMR or other inflammation, and interpret an ESR ≥100 mm/h in context rather than as proof of one diagnosis.

mnemonic.text: STACKED COINS SINK. Fibrinogen is the GLUE that stacks the coins (rouleaux); fewer coins (anaemia) fall faster; coins the wrong shape (sickle cells, spheres) will not stack; too many coins (polycythaemia) jam the column; and a TILTED tube lets the stack slide.
mnemonic.explanation: Ties the raising and lowering factors to rouleaux formation and column crowding.
mnemonic.limitation: Vibration and sample age also change the result, and ambient temperature may too; automated methods that extrapolate from shorter readings can differ from Westergren; and the ESR never identifies which disease is present.

analogyLimitations: The tube and rouleaux drawing is schematic, not to scale.
Age-based upper limits are rough rules; laboratories set their own reference intervals.
takeaway: The Westergren sedimentation rate measures how fast rouleaux fall in a vertical citrated tube in one hour, so red cell number and shape, fibrinogen and tilt all move it, a normal value does not exclude inflammation, and a value of 100 or more demands a search for its cause.

questions.stem: A patient with active osteomyelitis has an unexpectedly low ESR. Which coexisting condition best explains it?

options.rationale: Correct. Sickle cells inhibit rouleaux formation, which lowers the ESR.
Incorrect. Anaemia tends to raise the ESR, because fewer red cells settle faster.
Incorrect. Pregnancy raises fibrinogen and increases the ESR.
Incorrect. Renal disease is associated with raised, not lowered, ESR values.

questions.stem: A Westergren tube is found leaning slightly (about 3°) from vertical at the 60-minute reading. What is the expected effect?

options.rationale: Correct. Tilting accelerates sedimentation; a 3° tilt has been reported to raise the ESR by about 30%.
Incorrect. Tilt speeds the fall of the red cells; it does not slow it.
Incorrect. Even a small tilt from vertical increases the result.

options.text: Effect only on samples older than 6 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. Delayed testing lowers ESR separately; the tilt effect does not depend on sample age.

questions.stem: A man with known colon cancer develops fever, and his ESR is 112 mm/h. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: A marked elevation that is highly specific for significant disease; metastasis is possible, but infection must be sought
options.rationale: Correct. ESR ≥100 has high specificity and low sensitivity; infection is its commonest cause, although in adults with solid tumours it is often associated with metastasis.

options.text: Proof of metastatic spread; no further work-up is needed
options.rationale: Incorrect. ESR is nonspecific and cannot prove metastasis; with fever, infection must be considered.
Incorrect. Age-related rises are modest; 112 mm/h is far above any age-adjusted limit.

options.text: A sensitive screen showing cancer is present
options.rationale: Incorrect. The sensitivity of ESR ≥100 for malignancy is low (about 0.25 in one large series).

references.usedFor: ESR higher in women and rising with age in a general adult population; ESR tends to be higher with anaemia; haemoglobin concentration a strong determinant.

references.citation: Abbag FI, Al Qahtani JM. Extreme elevation of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate in children. Ann Saudi Med. 2007;27(3):175-178. doi:10.5144/0256-4947.2007.175

references.usedFor: ESR not raised at diagnosis in 7–22% of PMR patients, in whom CRP is usually raised; PMR and biopsy-proven GCA can occur with normal ESR and CRP.

claims.text: Westergren: 4:1 dilution with 0.105 M citrate, 200-mm vertical tube, read at 60 min.
Fibrinogen/globulins neutralise red-cell charge, causing rouleaux; three phases.

Raising factors (fibrinogen, anaemia, age, female sex, pregnancy, renal disease) and lowering factors (polycythaemia, sickle cells, spherocytes, low fibrinogen, liver disease, delayed testing); age-based rough limits.
A 3° tilt reported to raise ESR by about 30%; vibration raises ESR.
claims.note: The 30% figure appears in Amponsah 2026 as a secondary statement citing an earlier source; the original measurement study was not read.

claims.text: ESR rises in 24–48 h and falls slowly; CRP more sensitive, falls over about 18–20 h (close to its half-life).
Normal ESR in 7–22% of PMR at diagnosis; normal ESR does not exclude inflammation.
ESR ≥100: low sensitivity, high specificity, cause found in about 90%; infection commonest; in adults with solid tumours often associated with metastasis.
Reviewer: temporal arteritis/polymyalgia rheumatica typically run >90 mm/h.
claims.note: No open source read in this session supports a typical >90 mm/h value; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 31 Hit 11 says an ESR >100 mm/h in a known cancer patient usually means metastases. Open sources describe ESR ≥100 in adults with solid tumours as often associated with metastasis, but infection is the commonest cause of ESR ≥100 and its sensitivity for malignancy is low; the lesson teaches that infection must be sought (register flag rv-esr-100-cancer).

Ch. 31 Hit 11 says temporal arteritis/polymyalgia rheumatica typically run >90 mm/h. No open source read supports this figure, and Manzo 2018 reports a normal ESR in 7–22% of PMR at diagnosis; the figure is not taught.

morphology.note: No images; tube and factors shown as cards.

verification.notes: 7 factual claims checked against Tuzcu 2026, Lorubbio 2024, Amponsah 2026, Markanday 2015, Alende-Castro 2019, Abbag 2007, Manzo 2018 and Sproston 2018 (all read as Europe PMC full text); 1 pending (GCA/PMR >90 mm/h, not taught). The ICSH ESR recommendations themselves were not open access and were not read. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
